title: Conversation Glue
description: Sixteen high-utility hiragana words and expressions for reacting, clarifying, and keeping an everyday conversation moving.

words.meaningMnemonic: Zo runs a bakery whose front door is made of dough. When a guest hesitates, Zo swings it open and offers a bun with a cheerful <reading>DOUGH—ZO!</reading>: <vocabulary>please</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>go ahead</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>here you go</vocabulary> all happen in one gesture. どうぞ offers or encourages an object or action; in どうぞ〜てください, ください carries the request while どうぞ adds polite encouragement.

contextSentences.ja: こちらの席へどうぞ。
contextSentences.en: Please take this seat.

contextSentences.ja: コーヒーを入れました。どうぞ。
contextSentences.en: I made some coffee. Here you go.

contextSentences.ja: 「このパソコン、先に使ってもいいですか？」「はい、どうぞ」
contextSentences.en: “May I use this computer first?” “Yes, go ahead.”

words.meaningMnemonic: Picture a puppy that can parry anything you throw. You try one more newspaper: <reading>YAP—PARRY!</reading> Of course it blocks it again—<vocabulary>as expected</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>after all</vocabulary>, your first hunch was right. Use やっぱり when reality confirms your suspicion or when you return to an earlier conclusion.

contextSentences.ja: やっぱりこの店のカレーはおいしい。
contextSentences.en: As expected, this restaurant's curry is delicious.

contextSentences.ja: 電車で行こうと思ったけど、やっぱり歩いて行く。
contextSentences.en: I thought I'd take the train, but after all, I'll walk.

words.meaningMnemonic: A fussy turtle tastes the curry and groans, <reading>YUCK—CURRY!</reading> It pushes the bowl away so <vocabulary>slowly</vocabulary> that lunch lasts all afternoon, completely <vocabulary>at leisure</vocabulary>. ゆっくり describes doing something unhurriedly and can also mean relaxing or taking one's time.

contextSentences.ja: 今日は家でゆっくり休みます。
contextSentences.en: I'm going to relax at home today.

contextSentences.ja: もう一度、ゆっくり話してください。
contextSentences.en: Please say that again slowly.

contextSentences.ja: 時間はあるので、ご飯をゆっくり食べましょう。
contextSentences.en: We have time, so let's take our time eating.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>JAW</reading> blocks the hallway while everyone debates where to go. The jaw finally points left, snaps once, and the group says, <vocabulary>well then</vocabulary>—<vocabulary>in that case</vocabulary>—we go left. じゃあ is a casual transition to a decision or next step; では is more formal.

contextSentences.ja: じゃあ、駅で七時に会おう。
contextSentences.en: Well then, let's meet at the station at seven.

contextSentences.ja: 明日は雨なの？じゃあ、傘を持って行く。
contextSentences.en: Is it going to rain tomorrow? In that case, I'll take an umbrella.

words.meaningMnemonic: Moe opens a box and a living lump of dough leaps out to fix her broken chair. <reading>DOUGH, MOE!</reading> she cries, giving it a quick <vocabulary>thanks</vocabulary>, though <vocabulary>somehow</vocabulary> she has no idea why the dough can use tools. どうも alone is a casual, abbreviated thank-you; as an adverb it can express an uncertain ‘somehow’ or ‘for some reason.’

contextSentences.ja: 手伝ってくれて、どうも。
contextSentences.en: Thanks for helping me.

contextSentences.ja: 昨日はどうもありがとうございました。
contextSentences.en: Thank you so much for yesterday.

contextSentences.ja: どうも、この時計は五分遅れているようです。
contextSentences.en: It seems this clock is running five minutes slow.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a children's magic show, the magician announces a <reading>MASSACRE</reading> and raises a sword over a cake. The audience screams <vocabulary>no way</vocabulary>—<vocabulary>surely not</vocabulary>—until he slices only the cake and showers everyone with sprinkles. まさか expresses strong disbelief and often appears with a negative expectation; do not use it for a calm factual ‘unlikely.’

contextSentences.ja: まさか彼が来るとは思わなかった。
contextSentences.en: I never thought he would come.

contextSentences.ja: 「彼が優勝したよ。」「まさか！」
contextSentences.en: “He won.” “No way!”

words.meaningMnemonic: Two singers named Solo stand frozen under the spotlight, each waiting for the other to begin. The crowd stomps and chants <reading>SOLO, SOLO!</reading>: it is <vocabulary>about time</vocabulary>, and the song needs to start <vocabulary>soon</vocabulary>. そろそろ signals that the appropriate time is approaching, often before leaving, starting, or changing activity.

contextSentences.ja: そろそろ出かける時間です。
contextSentences.en: It's about time to leave.

contextSentences.ja: そろそろ電車が来るころです。
contextSentences.en: The train should be arriving soon.

words.meaningMnemonic: A choir's sheet music says <reading>CHANT—OH!</reading>, but one singer keeps improvising ‘uh.’ The conductor makes everyone redo it <vocabulary>properly</vocabulary>, and this time every singer hits ‘oh’ <vocabulary>without fail</vocabulary>. ちゃんと stresses that something is done correctly, reliably, or as expected.

contextSentences.ja: 宿題はちゃんと終わらせた？
contextSentences.en: Did you finish your homework properly?

contextSentences.ja: 明日はちゃんと時間どおりに来てね。
contextSentences.en: Make sure you arrive on time tomorrow.

words.meaningMnemonic: A tiny bird with a <reading>NARROW BEAK</reading> must empty a giant sack of seeds before sunset. It cannot grab many at once, but it carries <vocabulary>as much as possible</vocabulary> on every trip and promises to finish <vocabulary>if possible</vocabulary>. なるべく sets a practical best-effort limit rather than an absolute guarantee.

contextSentences.ja: なるべく早く返事してください。
contextSentences.en: Please reply as soon as possible.

contextSentences.ja: 野菜はなるべく毎日食べるようにしています。
contextSentences.en: I try to eat vegetables every day whenever possible.

words.meaningMnemonic: Nan finds that every square on her calendar has been renamed <reading>NAN DAY</reading>. She grabs the calendar and demands <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>—<vocabulary>how come</vocabulary> every day belongs to her, and <vocabulary>what for</vocabulary>? なんで is casual and conversational; どうして or なぜ can sound more neutral or formal depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: なんでそんなに急いでいるの？
contextSentences.en: Why are you in such a hurry?

contextSentences.ja: なんで昨日は電話に出なかったの？
contextSentences.en: How come you didn't answer the phone yesterday?

words.meaningMnemonic: A baker opens the oven and the dough she tests explodes into a balloon. She points at the <reading>DOUGH SHE TESTS</reading> and cries, <vocabulary>why</vocabulary>—<vocabulary>for what reason</vocabulary> did bread learn to fly? どうして asks for a reason; intonation can make it sound curious, surprised, or upset.

contextSentences.ja: どうして日本語を勉強しているんですか。
contextSentences.en: Why are you studying Japanese?

contextSentences.ja: どうしてドアが開かないんだろう。
contextSentences.en: I wonder why the door won't open.

words.meaningMnemonic: A sailor launches a yacht baked entirely from bread. When it floats, the dockworkers poke it and ask, <reading>DOUGH YACHT, EH?</reading>—<vocabulary>how</vocabulary> did you do that, and <vocabulary>by what means</vocabulary> is it still dry? どうやって asks about the method used to do something, not the reason it was done.

contextSentences.ja: 空港までどうやって行きますか。
contextSentences.en: How will you get to the airport?

contextSentences.ja: この漢字はどうやって入力するの？
contextSentences.en: How do you type this kanji?

words.meaningMnemonic: Nan straps a tuning dial to a pigeon's beak; the dial reads <reading>NAN—TONE A—COO</reading>. She turns it once and, <vocabulary>somehow</vocabulary>, the bird becomes an opera star even though she did it <vocabulary>for no particular reason</vocabulary>. なんとなく describes a vague cause, feeling, or impulse you cannot clearly explain.

contextSentences.ja: 今日はなんとなく散歩したい。
contextSentences.en: For some reason, I feel like taking a walk today.

contextSentences.ja: この曲を聞くと、なんとなく子どものころを思い出す。
contextSentences.en: This song somehow reminds me of my childhood.

words.meaningMnemonic: A diplomat unveils a <reading>CHINA MINI</reading>, a teacup-sized model of the whole country, in the middle of an unrelated meeting. Everyone pauses for the tiny side exhibit—<vocabulary>by the way</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>incidentally</vocabulary>, it even has working trains—then returns to the main topic. ちなみに introduces relevant extra information, not a completely unrelated subject change.

contextSentences.ja: 今日は通常どおり営業します。ちなみに、明日は店が休みです。
contextSentences.en: The shop is open as usual today. By the way, it'll be closed tomorrow.

contextSentences.ja: 私は辛い物が好きです。ちなみに、妹は甘い物が好きです。
contextSentences.en: I like spicy food. Incidentally, my younger sister likes sweets.

words.meaningMnemonic: A clerk receives a hundred-page letter addressed <reading>TO MURRAY</reading>. He crushes it into one sticky note: <vocabulary>in short</vocabulary>, Murray owes a llama; <vocabulary>in other words</vocabulary>, that is the whole point. つまり introduces a summary or logical conclusion, not a random change of topic.

contextSentences.ja: 会員しか入れません。つまり、先に登録が必要です。
contextSentences.en: Only members may enter. In other words, you need to register first.

contextSentences.ja: 電車もバスも止まっています。つまり、今日は歩くしかありません。
contextSentences.en: The trains and buses have stopped. In short, we have no choice but to walk today.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a rope bridge, Moe points to her nervous sheep and begins, <reading>MOE—SHE...</reading> The sheep pictures what happens <vocabulary>if</vocabulary> the bridge breaks, <vocabulary>supposing</vocabulary> she suddenly learns to fly. もし marks a hypothetical condition and commonly pairs with forms such as 〜たら; the sentence can often work without it.

contextSentences.ja: もし雨が降ったら、家にいます。
contextSentences.en: If it rains, I'll stay home.

contextSentences.ja: もし時間があれば、一緒に昼ご飯を食べませんか。
contextSentences.en: If you have time, would you like to have lunch together?

title: Food & Eating Out
description: Sixteen kana staples for meals, menus, restaurant visits, and common foods, mixing native hiragana terms with everyday loanwords.

words.meaningMnemonic: Your cousin bursts into dinner balancing tiny plates around a king-sized rice bowl. You shout <reading>OH, CUZ!</reading> as every plate becomes an おかず, a <vocabulary>side dish</vocabulary> supporting the rice. おかず normally means food eaten with rice, not simply any item located on the side.

contextSentences.ja: 今日のおかずは焼き魚です。
contextSentences.en: Today's side dish is grilled fish.

contextSentences.ja: お弁当のおかずに卵焼きを入れました。
contextSentences.en: I put rolled omelet in the bento as a side dish.

words.meaningMnemonic: At dinner, Chef Oka keeps handing Wally a fresh bowl every time he empties one. <reading>OKA—WALLY</reading> becomes the call for a <vocabulary>second helping</vocabulary>, and then Wally holds up his glass for a <vocabulary>refill</vocabulary>. おかわり is another serving of the same food or drink; おかわりする means to have seconds.

contextSentences.ja: ご飯をおかわりしてもいいですか。
contextSentences.en: May I have another serving of rice?

contextSentences.ja: コーヒーのおかわりはいかがですか。
contextSentences.en: Would you like a refill of coffee?

words.meaningMnemonic: Chef Sah-Mah serves a mountain of goat cheese, and every guest devours it. You pat your full stomach and call, <reading>GOAT CHEESE—OH, SAH-MAH!</reading> before bowing: <vocabulary>thank you for the meal</vocabulary>—<vocabulary>that was delicious</vocabulary>. ごちそうさま is said after eating to acknowledge the meal and those who provided it; before eating, use いただきます.

contextSentences.ja: ごちそうさま。とてもおいしかったです。
contextSentences.en: Thank you for the meal. It was delicious.

contextSentences.ja: 今日はごちそうさまでした。今度は私がおごるね。
contextSentences.en: Thanks for treating me today. I'll treat you next time.

words.readingMap: ご・ち・そ・う・さ・ま

words.meaningMnemonic: A river of <reading>CURRY</reading> bursts from a restaurant and floods a mountain of rice. Diners paddle through the spicy <vocabulary>curry</vocabulary> in naan-shaped boats until every plate is covered. In Japan, カレー often means Japanese-style curry served with rice; more specific dishes add a modifier such as カレーうどん.

contextSentences.ja: 今夜は辛いカレーを作ります。
contextSentences.en: I'm making spicy curry tonight.

contextSentences.ja: このカレーは子どもでも食べられる辛さです。
contextSentences.en: This curry is mild enough for children to eat.

words.meaningMnemonic: A chef yells <reading>SALAD!</reading> and a tornado of lettuce, tomatoes, and cucumbers dives into one bowl. The vegetables land perfectly dressed as a <vocabulary>salad</vocabulary>. サラダ covers salads broadly, including potato or macaroni salad, not only leafy greens.

contextSentences.ja: サラダにドレッシングをかけます。
contextSentences.en: I put dressing on the salad.

contextSentences.ja: ランチにはサラダとスープが付きます。
contextSentences.en: Lunch comes with a salad and soup.

words.meaningMnemonic: A magician drops a spoon into an empty bowl and shouts <reading>SOUP!</reading> Steam erupts and fills the room as warm <vocabulary>soup</vocabulary> pours over the rim. スープ usually refers to Western-style soup; 汁 is common in names of Japanese broths such as 味噌汁.

contextSentences.ja: このスープはまだ熱いです。
contextSentences.en: This soup is still hot.

contextSentences.ja: パンをスープにつけて食べました。
contextSentences.en: I dipped the bread in the soup before eating it.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant orange squeezes itself into a glass while shouting <reading>JUICE!</reading> The machine beside it also pours cola, because Japanese ジュース can label sweet <vocabulary>juice</vocabulary> or a <vocabulary>soft drink</vocabulary>. In everyday Japanese, ジュース is broader than English ‘juice,’ so check whether the drink is actually fruit-based.

contextSentences.ja: オレンジジュースを一つください。
contextSentences.en: One orange juice, please.

contextSentences.ja: 子どもたちは自動販売機で炭酸ジュースを買いました。
contextSentences.en: The children bought fizzy drinks from the vending machine.

words.meaningMnemonic: A wedding <reading>CAKE</reading> grows legs and runs away with every candle still burning. The guests tackle the runaway <vocabulary>cake</vocabulary> before it reaches the door, saving dessert. ケーキ is the general loanword for cake; compounds such as チーズケーキ specify the kind.

contextSentences.ja: 誕生日にチョコレートケーキを食べました。
contextSentences.en: I ate chocolate cake on my birthday.

contextSentences.ja: ケーキを六つに切り分けてください。
contextSentences.en: Please cut the cake into six pieces.

words.meaningMnemonic: An ice-cream cone puts on a badge marked <reading>ICE</reading> and freezes everything it touches. At the dessert counter, that badge usually means <vocabulary>ice cream</vocabulary>, though before another word it can mean <vocabulary>ice</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>iced</vocabulary>. アイス by itself commonly means ice cream; use 氷 for a chunk of ordinary ice.

contextSentences.ja: 暑いから、アイスを買おう。
contextSentences.en: It's hot, so let's buy ice cream.

contextSentences.ja: コーヒーはアイスとホット、どちらにしますか。
contextSentences.en: Would you like your coffee iced or hot?

words.meaningMnemonic: A tiny <reading>RESTAURANT</reading> unfolds from a menu and expands around you, trapping you at a table with a waiter. Since the whole building appeared to serve meals, it can only be a <vocabulary>restaurant</vocabulary>. レストラン generally suggests a Western-style or general restaurant, while specialized eateries may use 店 or 屋 names.

contextSentences.ja: 駅の近くに新しいレストランができました。
contextSentences.en: A new restaurant opened near the station.

contextSentences.ja: このレストランは予約したほうがいいですよ。
contextSentences.en: You should make a reservation at this restaurant.

words.meaningMnemonic: A waiter unrolls a <reading>MENUUU!</reading> so long that its final sound and the paper both stretch across the room. Every table it passes adds another dish to the <vocabulary>menu</vocabulary>. メニュー means a list of dishes or options; it does not by itself mean a fixed set meal.

contextSentences.ja: メニューを見せてください。
contextSentences.en: Please show me the menu.

contextSentences.ja: コーチが試合に向けた練習メニューを組んだ。
contextSentences.en: The coach planned a training program for the upcoming match.

contextSentences.ja: 設定は画面右上のメニューから変えられます。
contextSentences.en: You can change the settings from the menu at the top right of the screen.

words.meaningMnemonic: A dragon ignores dinner and guards a glittering <reading>DESSERT</reading> cart instead. When anyone reaches for the sweet final course, it breathes caramel to protect the <vocabulary>dessert</vocabulary>. デザート is the after-meal sweet course; お菓子 is broader for sweets and snacks.

contextSentences.ja: デザートは別腹です。
contextSentences.en: There's always room for dessert.

contextSentences.ja: 食後のデザートに果物を用意しました。
contextSentences.en: I prepared some fruit for dessert after the meal.

words.meaningMnemonic: A chef lassos a runaway tomato with one strand of <reading>PASTA</reading>. He reels it into a bowl where spaghetti and penne cheer for their fellow <vocabulary>pasta</vocabulary>. パスタ is the broad category; スパゲッティ names spaghetti specifically.

contextSentences.ja: ランチにトマトソースのパスタを注文しました。
contextSentences.en: I ordered pasta with tomato sauce for lunch.

contextSentences.ja: パスタは少しかためにゆでてください。
contextSentences.en: Please cook the pasta so it is still slightly firm.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>PIZZA</reading> spins like a flying saucer and splatters cheese across the ceiling. Everyone slices the landed <vocabulary>pizza</vocabulary> before it can take off again. ピザ is the standard word for pizza; ピッツァ sometimes appears for a more Italian-style pronunciation or product.

contextSentences.ja: このピザを三人で分けよう。
contextSentences.en: Let's split this pizza among the three of us.

contextSentences.ja: ピザを一枚、家まで配達してもらいました。
contextSentences.en: I had a pizza delivered to my home.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>SANDWICH</reading> snaps shut like a book, trapping the chef between two slices of bread. The filling—and the chef—make it unmistakably a <vocabulary>sandwich</vocabulary>. サンドイッチ is the full word; サンド is a common shorter form in food names.

contextSentences.ja: 朝ご飯に卵のサンドイッチを作りました。
contextSentences.en: I made an egg sandwich for breakfast.

contextSentences.ja: 公園で食べるサンドイッチを買ってきたよ。
contextSentences.en: I bought a sandwich to eat at the park.

words.readingMap: サ・ン・ド・イ・ッ・チ

words.meaningMnemonic: A bartender pulls a tap labeled <reading>BEEEER!</reading>, and the long stream fills a glass until foam buries the counter. The overflowing drink is unmistakably <vocabulary>beer</vocabulary>. ビール means beer; 生ビール specifies draft beer, and ビア also appears in compounds.

contextSentences.ja: 仕事の後で冷たいビールを飲みました。
contextSentences.en: I drank a cold beer after work.

contextSentences.ja: 生ビールをもう一杯お願いします。
contextSentences.en: One more draft beer, please.

title: Daily Tech & Errands
description: Sixteen katakana words heard constantly around devices, transport, shopping, work, and the home.

words.meaningMnemonic: A smartphone climbs into a paper cutter with its long name, スマートフォン, printed down its back. The blades keep <reading>スマ＋ホ</reading> and fling the rest away, leaving a pocket-sized <vocabulary>smartphone</vocabulary> called スマホ. スマホ is the ordinary casual abbreviation; スマートフォン is the full form.

contextSentences.ja: スマホの充電が切れました。
contextSentences.en: My smartphone ran out of charge.

contextSentences.ja: スマホで地図を見ながら駅まで歩きました。
contextSentences.en: I walked to the station while checking the map on my smartphone.

words.meaningMnemonic: A personal computer tries to carry its enormous name, パーソナルコンピューター, through a narrow office door. The door shears it down to <reading>パソ＋コン</reading>, and the shortened machine rolls to a desk as a <vocabulary>PC</vocabulary>. パソコン is the everyday Japanese word for a personal computer, especially a laptop or desktop rather than a phone.

contextSentences.ja: パソコンで資料を作っています。
contextSentences.en: I'm preparing the materials on my computer.

contextSentences.ja: パソコンが急に動かなくなりました。
contextSentences.en: My computer suddenly stopped working.

words.meaningMnemonic: An application icon sees the huge word アプリケーション and attacks it with scissors. It saves only <reading>アプリケーション → アプリ</reading>, then hops onto your phone as an <vocabulary>app</vocabulary>. アプリ is the normal abbreviation for a software application, especially on a phone or computer.

contextSentences.ja: このアプリは無料で使えます。
contextSentences.en: You can use this app for free.

contextSentences.ja: 写真を編集するアプリを入れました。
contextSentences.en: I installed an app for editing photos.

words.meaningMnemonic: A fisher casts a glowing <reading>NET</reading> over the city and catches every computer in it. The connected machines begin searching and streaming through the <vocabulary>Internet</vocabulary>, the <vocabulary>net</vocabulary>. ネット commonly abbreviates インターネット; in compounds it can also refer to a physical net or network.

contextSentences.ja: ネットで電車の時間を調べました。
contextSentences.en: I checked the train times online.

contextSentences.ja: 社内ネットワークにつながらないので、担当者に連絡しました。
contextSentences.en: I couldn't connect to the company network, so I contacted the person in charge.

contextSentences.ja: テニスのボールがネットに当たりました。
contextSentences.en: The tennis ball hit the net.

words.meaningMnemonic: A tiny envelope yells <reading>MAIL!</reading>, grows propellers, and flies from your phone into a friend's screen. It lands as an <vocabulary>email</vocabulary> or digital <vocabulary>message</vocabulary>, not a paper letter. メール usually means email or electronic messaging; 郵便 is used for postal mail.

contextSentences.ja: あとでメールを送ります。
contextSentences.en: I'll send an email later.

contextSentences.ja: 駅に着いたらメールしてね。
contextSentences.en: Message me when you get to the station.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>CAMERA</reading> sprouts one huge eye and chases you through a market. Each blink traps another scene as a photograph, proving the monster is a <vocabulary>camera</vocabulary>. カメラ is used for still or video cameras; the context tells which.

contextSentences.ja: 旅行にカメラを持って行きます。
contextSentences.en: I'm taking a camera on the trip.

contextSentences.ja: 猫にカメラを向けると、逃げてしまいました。
contextSentences.en: When I pointed the camera at the cat, it ran away.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>EARPHONE</reading> grows a pair of ears and tries to stuff itself into them. It splits into two tiny <vocabulary>earbuds</vocabulary>, one for each ear, so the music finally plays. イヤホン generally means in-ear earphones or earbuds; over-ear headphones are ヘッドホン.

contextSentences.ja: 電車の中ではイヤホンを使ってください。
contextSentences.en: Please use earphones on the train.

contextSentences.ja: 片方のイヤホンから音が聞こえません。
contextSentences.en: I can't hear anything through one of the earbuds.

words.meaningMnemonic: A superhero named <reading>AIR-CON</reading> punches a hole in a heat wave and blows cold air into the room. Everyone crowds around the victorious <vocabulary>air conditioner</vocabulary> as the temperature falls. エアコン refers to an air-conditioning unit and often includes both cooling and heating functions.

contextSentences.ja: 暑いので、エアコンをつけてもいいですか。
contextSentences.en: It's hot, so may I turn on the air conditioner?

contextSentences.ja: 寝る前にエアコンを消しました。
contextSentences.en: I turned off the air conditioner before going to bed.

words.meaningMnemonic: A long REMOTE CONTROL walks into a shrink ray and emerges with only <reading>REMO-CON</reading> on its cape. From the sofa, the tiny hero points at the TV and acts as the <vocabulary>remote control</vocabulary>. リモコン is a Japanese clipping of リモートコントロール and can control appliances beyond televisions.

contextSentences.ja: テレビのリモコンはどこですか。
contextSentences.en: Where is the TV remote?

contextSentences.ja: リモコンの電池を交換したら、また使えるようになりました。
contextSentences.en: After I replaced the remote's batteries, it started working again.

words.meaningMnemonic: A board marked <reading>GAME</reading> sucks everyone nearby onto its squares. They cannot escape until somebody wins the <vocabulary>game</vocabulary> by reaching the final space. ゲーム covers video, board, and other games; 試合 is more natural for many organized sports matches.

contextSentences.ja: 友だちとオンラインゲームをしました。
contextSentences.en: I played an online game with a friend.

contextSentences.ja: 家族でカードゲームを楽しみました。
contextSentences.en: My family and I enjoyed a card game.

words.meaningMnemonic: A <reading>TICKET</reading> sprouts teeth and bites anyone trying to enter without it. Once you show the pass, the little <vocabulary>ticket</vocabulary> unlocks the cinema door and lets you through. チケット is used for admission and travel tickets; 切符 is especially common for train or bus fares.

contextSentences.ja: 映画のチケットを二枚買いました。
contextSentences.en: I bought two movie tickets.

contextSentences.ja: 新幹線のチケットはスマホで予約できます。
contextSentences.en: You can book a bullet train ticket on your smartphone.

words.meaningMnemonic: A grocery store ties on a cape marked <reading>SUPER</reading> and grows until it covers an entire block. Shoppers race into the giant <vocabulary>supermarket</vocabulary> before the milk aisle stretches out of town. スーパー by itself usually means supermarket; before another word it can retain the sense ‘super.’

contextSentences.ja: 帰りにスーパーで牛乳を買います。
contextSentences.en: I'll buy milk at the supermarket on the way home.

contextSentences.ja: このスーパーは夜十時まで開いています。
contextSentences.en: This supermarket is open until ten at night.

words.meaningMnemonic: A cash register tries to print its full name, レジスター, but the receipt tears after the opening sound of <reading>REGISTER</reading>. The surviving レジ stamps a coin and becomes the shop's <vocabulary>cash register</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>checkout</vocabulary>. レジ can refer to the register, checkout area, or the worker at it depending on context.

contextSentences.ja: レジに長い列ができています。
contextSentences.en: A long line has formed at the checkout.

contextSentences.ja: このレジは故障中です。隣のレジをお使いください。
contextSentences.en: This register is out of order. Please use the next one.

contextSentences.ja: レジの人に袋はいらないと伝えました。
contextSentences.en: I told the cashier that I didn't need a bag.

words.meaningMnemonic: A walking <reading>TOILET</reading> squeezes through a doorway and loses the end of its name in the frame. Now labeled トイレ, it points desperate travelers toward the <vocabulary>restroom</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>bathroom</vocabulary>. トイレ is the everyday word for the toilet or restroom; it does not normally mean a room for bathing.

contextSentences.ja: すみません、トイレはどこですか。
contextSentences.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

contextSentences.ja: 次の駅でトイレを使いたいです。
contextSentences.en: I want to use the restroom at the next station.

words.meaningMnemonic: A giant <reading>BUS</reading> unfolds like an accordion and swallows a whole queue of passengers. It carries everyone along the route, so there is no mistaking the vehicle for anything but a <vocabulary>bus</vocabulary>. バス is the road vehicle in ordinary travel contexts; バス停 means bus stop.

contextSentences.ja: 毎朝バスで学校に通っています。
contextSentences.en: I commute to school by bus every morning.

contextSentences.ja: 最終バスに間に合いませんでした。
contextSentences.en: I missed the last bus.

words.meaningMnemonic: At a café, three workers wear name tags reading <reading>AL—BUY—TOE</reading>. Al stocks shelves, Buy runs the register, and Toe mops the floor during a short shift—the strangest <vocabulary>part-time job</vocabulary> Al has ever taken. アルバイト usually means a part-time job or worker; it comes from German Arbeit, not the English phrase in the memory hook.

contextSentences.ja: 週末はカフェでアルバイトをしています。
contextSentences.en: I work part-time at a café on weekends.

contextSentences.ja: この店では新しいアルバイトを二人募集しています。
contextSentences.en: This shop is hiring two new part-time workers.
